e.t: Beriah is a personal name, referring to an individual in Israel’s genealogical records. It is consistently rendered “Beriah” and appears eleven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Genesis, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. The word functions as a name rather than as a description or action. Its use is especially connected with family lines and recorded descent, including a birth or begetting event in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verse is needed to identify which person named Beriah is intended in a particular passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “queen,” referring to a woman who holds royal rank or status. It is used six times in the Old Testament, consistently describing a queen rather than a general female title. The word appears in accounts involving royal households and court speech, showing its normal use for a recognized woman of royal standing. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the queen being discussed.

This Hebrew word means “man” and functions as a noun, identifying a man rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Psalm 18:25. Its basic sense is therefore clear, while its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s identity, its single supported meaning, and its one occurrence are all reflected in the available records.

This Hebrew word means “cut.” It functions as a verb, describing an action performed on something or someone. In its Old Testament uses, the action may be expressed physically or through an official decision, so the surrounding sentence determines how the cutting is understood. The word occurs 13 times in the Hebrew Bible, including passages involving a king’s command, a physical cutting action, and a decree. Its central idea remains an intentional act that separates or removes something.

e.t: Corn is a Hebrew noun for the harvested crop or food produced from the land. It commonly appears as something God gives, people bring, receive, or depend on as provision. The word occurs 40 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah, so it describes an ordinary agricultural product rather than a rare or specialized object. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

e.t: Zimri is a Hebrew personal name, referring to particular people rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Old Testament, it identifies individuals in historical and genealogical passages. The name occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Bible corpus, including references in Numbers, 1 Kings, 1 Chronicles, 2 Kings, and Jeremiah. Its uses include people connected with family lines and accounts involving death, so the surrounding passage is needed to determine which Zimri is intended. The English form is a rendering of the name, not a separate descriptive meaning.

e.t: “Zerahiah” is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in genealogical records in 1 Chronicles and Ezra. The surrounding evidence places the name among family lines and identifies its bearer in those records. Thus, its ordinary function is to identify a person; its precise significance in any one passage comes from that passage’s context.

This Hebrew verb expresses having or seeing—holding something in view, perceiving it, or possessing it. Its normal sense depends on the sentence: it may describe what someone sees, beholds, or has. The word occurs 51 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it represents a recurring biblical idea rather than a rare expression. In passages about visions and judgment, it can concern what a person perceives; elsewhere, its rendering as “have” points to possession. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is intended.

This Hebrew word refers to Hamath, a place name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both occurrences appearing in 2 Chronicles 8:3. The word therefore identifies a location in the biblical record. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding context, but its basic lexical function is geographical: it names Hamath. This is a proper name, so readers should understand it as identifying a specific place rather than describing an action, quality, or person.

e.t: Hepher is a personal name, rendered “Hepher.” It identifies people in Israel’s genealogical and tribal records, including a descendant of Manasseh and a person connected with Judah’s family lines. The name occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always functioning as a proper name rather than as a description or action. Its appearances are associated with family descent, tribal inheritance, and recorded genealogies, so readers should understand it primarily as the name of a biblical person or family figure.

This Hebrew word describes someone as “afraid.” It is used as the sentence’s action or condition, showing that a person or group is afraid in the Old Testament. It occurs 39 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages involving different people and situations. The surrounding sentence and passage determine who is afraid, what prompts that condition, and how the word functions there. The word is found from Genesis through Zechariah.

e.t: “Jabin” is a personal name, identifying a particular man rather than expressing a general quality or action. In the Old Testament, it refers to a king associated with Hazor and to the king mentioned in the account of Deborah and Barak. The name occurs eight times in the Hebrew Bible, chiefly in Judges 4, and is also found in Joshua 11 and Psalm 83. Its precise significance in any individual passage comes from the surrounding context, but its normal function is simply to name Jabin.

This word refers to an “Izrahite,” functioning as a designation for a person identified by that name or group connection. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 27:8. Since the available wording provides the designation but not the surrounding verse text, the word’s basic meaning is clear while the particular person’s role must be learned from the passage itself.

Joktheel is a proper name, used for a named place rather than for an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Joshua 15:38 and once in 2 Kings 14:7. Its repeated English rendering is “Joktheel,” confirming that the word functions as a name. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain what is said about Joktheel in either passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “curtains”—fabric panels used as a covering or enclosure. In the Old Testament, it appears 54 times in 32 verses, with most occurrences in Exodus 26, where the text repeatedly discusses several curtains together and their arrangement. It can function as the object of actions involving making or speaking about it. This is a Hebrew noun referring to a tangible textile object rather than an abstract idea.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “any.” It functions as a term that leaves the particular item or person unspecified, rather than identifying one particular individual or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 19:28. Its role is connected with something being given or placed upon another, but the precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording. Thus, its basic contribution is to express an open or non-specific reference: “any,” without naming which one.

This Hebrew word expresses the action “fall.” It functions as an action word describing what someone or something does. In its three Old Testament occurrences, it is rendered “fall,” appearing twice in Proverbs and once in Hosea. Its surrounding relationships show it serving as the predicate—the part of a sentence that states what the subject does. The precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and its subject.

Meah is a Hebrew name used for a specific named entity rather than a general description. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice, both times in Nehemiah, and is rendered “Meah.” The available references place it in Nehemiah 3:1 and Nehemiah 12:39, but the surrounding verse text is not included here, so its precise role in either passage cannot be described further. Its meaning is therefore best expressed by preserving the name Meah rather than assigning it an unsupported synonym.

This Hebrew word means “mixed.” It describes something made up of different elements brought together rather than remaining pure or separate. Its exact force in a sentence depends on what is being described, but the central idea is combination. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 1:22, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated examples in this corpus.

The Hebrew word means “slaughter.” It refers to killing as an act or result, naming what is intended or brought about. It appears once in the Old Testament corpus, in Isaiah 14:21. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its exact force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its basic lexical meaning remains “slaughter,” without requiring a broader or different sense.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to prey or something taken, especially what is seized or carried away. It can describe what has been captured in a conflict and is treated as an object of taking. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, chiefly in Numbers and Isaiah, with one occurrence in Psalms. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is what has been taken or secured.

This Hebrew noun means “chaff,” the light, unwanted material separated from grain. In the Old Testament, it is used for something insubstantial and easily scattered or carried away. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages in Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Hosea, and Zephaniah. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains chaff: material without the enduring substance of grain.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “burden.” It is used as a noun for something carried, presented, or assigned. In the Old Testament, it occurs 16 times and can refer to a burden brought before someone, given as an offering or gift, or connected with a visible sign. Its central idea remains something placed upon or brought to another, whether physically or in a matter requiring attention. The exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “rule.” It describes the exercise of governing authority over people or a realm. In the Old Testament, it is used of rulers and kings, and it can describe God’s dominion as well. Its central idea is the direction and oversight of those under a ruler’s authority. The word occurs 82 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that ruling is a recurring biblical subject rather than a rare or specialized idea.

This word means “toward,” marking the direction or orientation of someone or something in relation to another point. It functions as a directional term, showing where an action, movement, or position is aimed. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Daniel 6:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and context, but its basic sense is a movement or orientation toward a person, place, or object.

This Hebrew word means “elevation.” It refers to being raised high and functions as a term naming that elevated state or position. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 48:2. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the word’s precise force in that verse cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains elevation: a height or raised standing expressed as a thing rather than an action.

Nahath is a personal name, rendered consistently as “Nahath” in the Hebrew Old Testament. It appears five times, in genealogical records and in a list connected with Judah’s administration. Because the available wording preserves it as a name rather than translating it into a descriptive term, these occurrences identify people named Nahath rather than establish a broader ordinary meaning for the word. Its precise significance as a name is not stated in the available passages.

This Hebrew word means “destroy” and functions as an action word describing what happens to something. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 42:14. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise force in that sentence must be understood from the passage itself. Its basic lexical sense remains the action of destroying, rather than a general description of an object, person, or quality.

Samgar-Nebo is a Hebrew proper name, identifying a named figure rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both occurrences being in Jeremiah 39:3. The name itself does not supply a broader everyday meaning, and without the verse text, its precise role in that sentence cannot be explained responsibly. In ordinary reading, treat it as a personal name.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “words.” It refers to the verbal content that is spoken, heard, received, or recorded. Scripture uses it in connection with speech, including words presented before others and words received as instruction. It occurs 49 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is a recurring term for meaningful verbal expression rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Adna is a personal name, not a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies people named Adna in the Old Testament’s Hebrew corpus. The name appears twice, once in Ezra 10:30 and once in Nehemiah 12:15. Since no broader lexical definition is provided, its clear meaning for a reader is the personal designation “Adna.” The surrounding verse context is needed to distinguish the individuals and explain their specific roles in those passages.

This Hebrew word means “bake,” describing the action of preparing food by heating it. It functions as a verb rather than naming an object or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 4:12. Its related wording there connects the baking action with grain and other ingredients, but the precise force of the instruction belongs to the surrounding verse and passage. The central idea remains straightforward: to cook food through baking.

“Gazites” is a noun used as a designation for people connected with Gaza. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs two times, appearing once in Joshua 13:3 and once in Judges 16:2. Its role is to identify a people group rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. The word’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context, but its basic function remains a personal or group designation.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Gomorrah,” referring to the city known by that name in the Old Testament. It functions as a place-name rather than a general description or action word. The word occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Scriptures, from Genesis through Zephaniah, and appears in passages that mention Gomorrah among particular cities and places. Its exact significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the city’s name.

This word means “tenth,” identifying one part in a division of ten. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used for a tenth portion or position, including measured offerings and ordered places. It occurs 29 times across 26 verses, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its normal sense is straightforward: something that is tenth, or amounts to a tenth, within the matter being described.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “green,” describing something that has a fresh, living color. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song of Solomon 2:13. Its use there is connected with the visible freshness of growing plants and the renewal associated with them, though the precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word’s basic sense remains simple: it identifies something green, fresh-looking, or connected with living growth.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “lightness,” referring to a quality of being light or lacking weight or seriousness. It appears once in the Old Testament, in Jeremiah 23:32. In that passage, it functions as the object of an action or command, so the surrounding verse determines the precise way this quality is being described. Its basic sense remains “lightness,” rather than a broad collection of unrelated meanings.

This Hebrew word means “certain.” It serves to identify someone or something as definite or known rather than unspecified. The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 8:13. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be explained further; its ordinary lexical sense remains a term expressing certainty or definiteness. This is a rare Hebrew word with a narrowly supported meaning.

Zuar is a Hebrew personal name, rendered as “Zuar.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and all five occurrences are in Numbers. Its repeated use in genealogical and tribal records shows its role as a personal designation within Israel’s recorded history. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain each specific reference.

e.t: The word means “venison,” referring to food obtained through hunting. As a Hebrew noun, it names the hunted food itself rather than the person who hunts. It functions as the object of statements and speech concerning hunting, food, and desire. This word occurs 17 times in the Old Testament, with many occurrences in Genesis. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word describes acting “humbly”—the manner of carrying oneself without self-exaltation. It functions as a description of how someone conducts an action, rather than naming a person, object, or event. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Proverbs and Micah, where the wording presents humility as a recognizable way of living before God. The central idea is a restrained, lowly posture expressed through one’s conduct. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

Kabzeel is the name of a place in the Old Testament. It appears three times in the Hebrew Bible corpus, rendered consistently as “Kabzeel,” rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. The name occurs in Joshua, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance cannot be stated beyond identifying this place. It is therefore a geographical name, not a general quality, action, or title.

“Ardites” is the name used for a people or family group in the Hebrew Old Testament. It occurs once, in Numbers 26:40, and functions as a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. Because the word appears only in this recorded setting and no verse text is supplied here, its precise relationship to the surrounding names belongs to the passage itself. Its basic meaning is therefore the identifying name “Ardites.”

This Hebrew word means “be.” It functions as a predicate, expressing that a person or thing is in a particular state or condition. In the Hebrew Bible data represented here, it occurs once, in Job 33:25. The word itself contributes the idea of being or existing in the stated condition, while the surrounding wording identifies what that condition is. Its role in the sentence is therefore to express the state or condition attributed to its subject.

This Hebrew word means “humble.” It functions as an action word, describing the lowering of a person or people rather than naming an object or quality. Its basic sense concerns taking, or being placed in, a low position. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears two times, in Psalm 68:30 and Proverbs 6:3. The surrounding verse determines whether the action is commanded or described.

This word refers to Mesopotamia, the region associated with the biblical accounts in which it appears. It functions as a geographic name rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs eight times in four verses, from Genesis through 1 Chronicles. The name identifies a place connected with several passages involving travel, ancestry, or foreign peoples, though the precise significance in any one verse depends on that passage’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “backsliding.” It describes a condition or pattern of departing from a faithful path. In the Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Its use in these passages presents “backsliding” as a recognizable spiritual condition rather than a single isolated act. The surrounding verse determines the specific force in each occurrence, but the central idea remains a person or people characterized by backsliding.

This Hebrew word means “hedge”: to place a barrier around or enclose something. It functions as a verb, describing protective or obstructive action rather than a physical object alone. In Job 1:10, it is associated with a hedge around Job, his household, and his possessions. In Hosea 2:6, the same word describes enclosing or blocking a path. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a consistent basic idea of setting a boundary that protects or prevents passage.

The word refers to “Shicron,” functioning as a proper name rather than a general descriptive term. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Joshua 15:11, so its meaning is primarily identifying rather than describing an action or quality. The available wording does not provide a broader lexical definition; therefore, Shicron is best understood as the name used for the location identified in that passage.

This Hebrew word means “fat.” It functions as a descriptive word, identifying a person, animal, land, or other thing as fat. In the Old Testament, it occurs ten times across several books, showing that this is a recurring word with a consistent basic sense rather than a term limited to one passage. Its precise role in a verse depends on the noun or subject it describes and the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Seir,” referring to a named place in the Old Testament. It appears 39 times across 38 verses, with references in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Chronicles, and Ezekiel. The name commonly functions as the object of movement, speech, giving, or other actions involving that place. Its meaning is therefore chiefly identifying rather than describing a quality or action. The surrounding passage determines what is happening at Seir in any particular verse.

Sarid is a Hebrew place name, referring to a location rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in Joshua, and is rendered “Sarid.” Since the available occurrences are place-name references, the word’s ordinary function is to identify a specific location within the land described in Joshua. Its precise significance in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the territorial description in which the name appears.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “law,” serving as the stated body of commands or requirements that God gives and people are expected to keep. It is used 222 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Malachi, and commonly appears in connection with obeying, keeping, rejecting, or receiving what God has commanded. Scripture also associates it with commandments in passages concerning worship, national life, and faithful obedience.

This word is a Hebrew proper name referring to “Taanach,” the name of a place in the Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or object; it identifies a location. The name appears seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in passages from Joshua, Judges, 1 Kings, and 1 Chronicles. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its historical setting.

Teresh is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Esther: 2:21 and 6:2. In English Bible renderings, the name is preserved as “Teresh,” so its meaning is best understood as the person’s name within those passages rather than as a translated description. The surrounding verse context is needed to explain the individual’s role in each occurrence.

This Hebrew word refers to “cisterns,” a place made to hold water. It is a concrete noun naming a water-storage place rather than the water itself. The word occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across three verses, including two occurrences in Jeremiah 2:13. Its basic sense is a physical container for water, while the surrounding sentence determines how that image functions in a particular passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to garments or clothing worn by people. It describes physical articles of dress, including clothing connected with ordinary life and with special occasions or duties. The word occurs 218 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it covers a broad range of clothing references rather than one narrowly defined item. Its use can also appear in descriptions of giving, wearing, removing, or changing garments, but the surrounding passage determines the particular significance in each verse.

This Hebrew word means “safely.” It functions as an adverb, describing an action or condition as taking place safely. It appears 42 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, across 41 verses, so it is a recurring word for expressing safety in different settings. Its relationships in passages concerning dwelling and divine action reinforce this practical use. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.
